KEY MESSAGE 1...High pressure brings continued cool and dry 
conditions

Broad high pressure over the Great Lakes strengthens to 
near/just above 1040mb as it pushes east across southern Ontario
and eventually into Atlantic Canada. 925mb temperatures 
continue to hover right around -3C or -4C today. supporting 
afternoon high temperatures in the 40s again. Expecting another 
night of decent radiational cooling with calm winds, although it
may be hampered somewhat by increasing cloudiness ahead of the 
coastal storm. Overnight lows likely in the low 20s for the 
higher elevations and upper 20s elsewhere (upper 30s for the 
Cape, Islands, and immediate Coast).

KEY MESSAGE 2...An impactful coastal storm Thanksgiving Day 
into Friday will bring dangerous marine conditions, strong 
winds, periods of heavy rainfall, and the potential for coastal 
flooding and beach erosion.

There hasn't been much deviation in the guidance over the past 
24 hours. A bit of good news for those with outdoor plans 
Thanksgiving morning, as guidance continues to favor a drier 
start to the holiday. The 00z HRRR holds off the onset of rain 
until 2-4 PM across southern portions of the region, while the 
RRFS is a bit faster, between 10 AM and 2 PM. Given the strong 
high pressure to our north and the dry air mass this system will
initially need to overcome, wouldn't be surprised to see the 
slower onset materialize. As previously discussed, a moisture-
rich southern stream shortwave will be absorbed by a more potent
northern stream shortwave, resulting in a deepening low lifting
west of southern New England. This, combined with a departing 
1040+ mb high, will result in a tight pressure gradient across 
the region.

Coastal Flooding: Astronomical tides are among the highest of 
the year, with Boston's midday high tides Thursday and Friday 
reaching 11.84 ft and 11.67 ft, respectively, compared to 9.89 
ft overnight (all water levels referenced to MLLW). Fortunately,
the strongest easterly winds continue to be favored around the 
lower high tide, though even a slight change in timing could 
make a rather significant difference in the extent of coastal 
flooding. The latest Stevens Institute guidance shows 
considerable uncertainty at the Fox Point Hurricane Barrier in 
Providence, with forecast water levels below 7 ft Thursday 
afternoon, though the 5th and 95th percentiles range from 5.5 to
8 ft. At Boston, forecast water levels are near 12 ft during 
all three high tide cycles, though the 95th percentile suggests 
12.5 to 13 ft is possible. Recall that coastal flooding impacts 
at Boston begin around 12.3 ft. At Nantucket, the greatest 
concern appears to be Friday's midday high tide, with water 
levels potentially reaching minor flood stage (5.5 ft). Even as 
winds diminish Friday, residual storm surge and wave action 
could still result in coastal flooding during the midday high 
tide. Additionally, significant wave action over multiple high 
tide cycles could lead to beach erosion. Conditions will likely 
warrant Coastal Flood Advisories for portions of the coastline, 
though for now will allow the day shift to reassess.

Marine: Dangerous marine conditions are anticipated Thursday 
into Friday, with seas potentially exceeding 20 ft. There is 
increasing ensemble support for storm-force gusts across the 
southern waters, with ECMWF ensemble probabilities of 50+ knot 
gusts approaching 60 percent near Block Island, while the GFS 
ensemble depicts more widespread probabilities of 50-70 percent 
across the southern waters. Will maintain the Storm Watches for 
the southern waters and Gale Watches for the eastern waters, 
including Boston Harbor and Narragansett Bay.

Wind: The signal for an anomalously strong easterly LLJ 
continues to be rather impressive, with NAEFS wind speed 
anomalies as high as 4-5 standard deviations above climatology 
Thursday. Additionally, the ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index (EFI) 
for wind gusts is generally 0.7 to 0.9 across much of southern 
New England, locally exceeding 0.9 (on a scale with an upper 
limit of 1.0). The 00z HRRR and RRFS depict a rather robust 925 
mb LLJ of 65-85 knots. However, one of the challenges continues 
to be how much of this momentum we can bring to the surface 
given the pronounced thermal inversion between 925 and 950 mb. 
Even if roughly half of those winds were realized at the 
surface, this would support advisory-level gusts. Still 
anticipating southeast to east gusts of 45-55 mph within the 
Wind Advisory area, with isolated gusts to 60 mph, while 
elsewhere gusts will generally be on the order of 30-40 mph. 
Given the uncertainty in momentum transfer, opted to maintain 
the existing Wind Advisories. Should the inversion weaken or 
winds aloft trend stronger, high wind headlines may need to be 
considered for Block Island, Cape Cod, and the Islands. Gusts
